lessons.title: Lesson 157: 경우 – Case or Circumstance
lessons.explanation: Original practice for the HTSK Lesson 157 focus. Use the official Unit 7 lesson for the full explanation and more examples.

cards.translation: In cases where communication is not smooth, contact the support team
cards.explanation:
경우 means a case, situation or circumstance. It is a noun that lets Korean single out the situation being discussed.

Use 경우 when you want to say ‘in the case of…’, ‘when…’ or ‘if…’, especially when describing a specific situation rather than simply naming a time.

Put a noun before 경우 with 의, or put an adjective or verb modifier before it: 한국의 경우, 불안한 경우, 비가 오는 경우. Add particles such as 에는 when the sentence needs them.

Use 경우 when you want to say ‘in the case of…’, ‘when…’ or ‘if…’, especially when describing a specific situation rather than simply naming a time.

Put a noun before 경우 with 의, or put an adjective or verb modifier before it: 한국의 경우, 불안한 경우, 비가 오는 경우. Add particles such as 에는 when the sentence needs them.

lessons.explanation: Original practice for the HTSK Lesson 163 focus. Use the official Unit 7 lesson for the full explanation and more examples.

cards.translation: This is a good example, you know
cards.explanation:
말이다 at the end of a sentence repeats, stresses or checks what has already been said. Depending on the quoted clause, it can mean ‘what I’m saying is…’ or ‘you mean…?’.

Use it in conversational speech to emphasize a statement, clarify what someone meant or check an interpretation. HTSK notes that a forceful tone can sound rude, so intonation matters.

Put the appropriate modifier or quoted form before 말이다: ~다는 말이야, ~(이)라는 말이야, ~느냐는 말이야, ~(으)라는 말이야 or ~자는 말이야. Use the informal endings shown in the lesson, such as 말이야 and 말이지.

lessons.title: Lesson 164: ~아/어야 말이지 – Expressing Annoyance
lessons.explanation: Original practice for the HTSK Lesson 164 focus. Use the official Unit 7 lesson for the full explanation and more examples.

cards.prompt: 경제도 어렵고 월급도 오르지 않아서 요즘 살맛이 나려면 좀 더 안정된 직장이 ___
cards.translation: The economy is bad, and my salary isn’t increasing, so for life to feel worthwhile, I need a more stable job, you know!
cards.explanation:
~아/어야 말이지 expresses that something has to happen, while adding the speaker’s frustration that this should be obvious. It is often rendered as ‘...has to happen, you know!’.

Use it when a necessary condition is missing or needs to be stressed, especially when the speaker is annoyed that they even have to point out this obvious requirement.

Attach ~아야 or ~어야 to a verb or adjective stem, then add 말이지: 하다 → 해야 말이지, 좋다 → 좋아야 말이지. The ending is usually conversational and can follow a longer context.

lessons.title: Lesson 165: ~(으)니/~기에 말이지 – Emphasizing Fortune or Relief
lessons.explanation: Original practice for the HTSK Lesson 165 focus. Use the official Unit 7 lesson for the full explanation and more examples.

cards.prompt: 반박을 정확히 ___ 아니었으면 논리에서 밀릴 뻔했어
cards.translation: It’s a good thing I refuted it accurately; otherwise, I might have lost in the argument
cards.explanation:
~(으)니 말이지 and ~기에 말이지 mark a fortunate reason: the first clause explains what prevented or avoided a bad result, with a feeling of relief.

Use them when something happened or was accomplished and, because of it, an unwanted event did not happen. The following clause often describes the hypothetical result that was avoided.

Attach ~(으)니 or ~기에 to the verb or adjective clause, then add 말이지: 챙겼으니 말이지, 깊기에 말이지. A following clause commonly uses 안 그랬으면, ~았/었을 거야 or ~ㄹ/을 뻔했어.

~ㄹ/을까 말까 means whether to do something or not and expresses indecision.

lessons.title: Humble response to praise
lessons.explanation: Original practice for the HTSK Lesson 174 focus. Use the official Unit 7 lesson for the full explanation and more examples.

cards.prompt: ___. 그냥 조명 때문에 그렇게 보이는 거예요.
cards.translation: High? It’s just the lighting that makes it look that way.
cards.explanation:
Korean can respond to praise with humble expressions such as ~기는요, downplaying or denying the compliment.

Use these forms when politely rejecting praise or showing modesty in conversation.

Attach ~기는요 to the praised predicate, or use the lexical humble reply shown by HTSK; the tone is conversational and polite.

lessons.title: No exceptions with ~치고
lessons.explanation: Original practice for the HTSK Lesson 175 focus. Use the official Unit 7 lesson for the full explanation and more examples.

cards.translation: Among Korean people, there isn’t one who doesn’t know the national anthem
cards.explanation:
~치고 means for a person or thing of that category, with the implication that there are no exceptions or that the example is notable.

Use it to make a generalization about a group or to say that an item is unusual for its category.

Attach 치고 to the noun, and use ~치고는 when contrasting the expectation with the actual result.
cards.source_sentence: 한국 사람치고 애국가를 모르는 사람이 없어요
